The Pied currawong (Strepera graculina) is a large passerine endemic to eastern Australia, where it occupies a diverse range of forested and urban habitats. Necropsies of captive-bred nestlings indicate that eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] yield hatchlings after approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days], a developmental period typical of many cracticids. The hatchlings emerge with a mass of 18.3 grams [Ww0 = 18.3 grams], a value that aligns closely with altricial neonates of similar body size. The initial wet weight of these young is modest relative to the adult form they will eventually achieve. The post-hatching environment is critical; the nestlings are brooded intensively for the first week and are dependent on biparental food delivery for the duration of the nestling stage. The mass gain during this period is rapid and is sustained by a diet dominated by arthropods and small vertebrates.

Adult females of the species attain a mean ultimate wet weight of 280 grams [Wwi = 280 grams], though field data from across their range indicate a broader span of 243 to 324 grams. Males are substantially heavier, with an average maximum adult body mass of 320.5 grams [Wwi = 320.5 grams] and a documented range of 259 to 385 grams. This degree of sexual size dimorphism is pronounced among Australian passerines and is thought to relate to differences in foraging tactics and territory defence. The adult body mass data were collected from museum specimen series and capture–recapture programs in New South Wales and Queensland. The warm-thermoneutral zone of adults has been characterized in laboratory respirometry trials conducted at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], and under these conditions, the basal oxygen consumption of resting individuals averages 339 milliliters per hour [JOi = 339 milliliters per hour]. This metabolic rate is consistent with predictions for a bird of this mass and reflects the species' active, socially dominant lifestyle.

The reproductive schedule of the Pied currawong is tightly seasonal, with most breeding activity concentrated in the austral spring and early summer. The maximum annual output is defined by a clutch of three eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of three eggs] and a single nesting attempt per year [F_R_i = single nesting attempt per year]. This reproductive rate is typical of a long-lived, slow-breeding forest corvoid. The eggs themselves are large and heavily pigmented, and incubation is shared between the sexes. The first successful brood of the year is generally initiated approximately one year from the female's own birth (approximately one year from birth) [tR = approximately one year from birth], indicating that individuals do not breed in their first calendar year of life at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Instead, there is a prolonged period of juvenile development and social maturation before the first reproductive investment. The incubation and brooding behaviours are highly coordinated, with the male provisioning the incubating female extensively during the laying and early incubation phases.

Key developmental milestones under field conditions at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] have been well documented for populations in the Southern Highlands of New South Wales. The fledging period, defined as the time from hatching to the achievement of sustained flight, lasts 31 days [tx = 31 days] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively short nestling phase is characteristic of many cracticids, whose young depart the nest while still dependent on parental care for several additional weeks. The onset of puberty, or gonadal maturation, occurs at 93 days after hatching [tp = 93 days after hatching], a timing that aligns with the post-fledging dependence phase and the gradual transition to independent foraging at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The attainment of full physiological competence for reproduction is therefore not immediate upon fledging but is deferred until the young bird has acquired sufficient foraging skills and body condition to support the energetic demands of nesting.

In terms of overall life-history pace, the Pied currawong is a relatively long-lived species, with maximum lifespan in the wild estimated at approximately 8800 days [am = approximately 8800 days] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This value, recorded at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], places it among the more durable of the Australian cracticids and reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and repeated breeding attempts over high annual fecundity. The combination of a modest clutch size, a delayed onset of first reproduction, and an extended reproductive lifespan suggests strong iteroparous selection in this species. The ecological implications are significant: populations can persist through periods of low food availability by relying on the survival of experienced adult breeders, a demographic buffer that is less available to shorter-lived, more fecund species. This longevity, together with the species' dietary flexibility, has allowed the Pied currawong to thrive in both intact forests and human-modified landscapes.
